label: Problem set 3
title: Problem set 3: Kinetics of electrode reactions
summary: Practice with the Tafel slope, exchange current density, standard rate constant, transfer coefficients and the high-field limit of Butler-Volmer.

intro.text: Chapter 3 turns the exponential current-overpotential relation into working formulas: the Tafel slope b = 2.303RT/(alpha n F), the exchange current density i0 = nFk0C, and the Tafel equation eta = b log10(i/i0).
At 25 C the prefactor 2.303RT/F is 0.05916 V, so for alpha = 0.5 and n = 1 the Tafel slope is near 0.118 V per decade.

blocks.text: Chapter 3 turns the exponential current-overpotential relation into working formulas: the Tafel slope b = 2.303RT/(alpha n F), the exchange current density i0 = nFk0C, and the Tafel equation eta = b log10(i/i0).
At 25 C the prefactor 2.303RT/F is 0.05916 V, so for alpha = 0.5 and n = 1 the Tafel slope is near 0.118 V per decade.

blocks.title: Tafel slope at 25 C
steps: Numerator 5708 J/mol; divide by 48242 C/mol gives 0.1183 V.

questions.question: Calculate the Tafel slope b = 2.303RT/(alpha n F) in volts per decade for alpha = 0.5, n = 1, T = 298.15 K, R = 8.314 J/(K mol), F = 96485 C/mol.
The exchange current density is i0 = nFk0C. Calculate i0 in microamperes per cm2 for n = 1, k0 = 1.0e-4 cm/s, C = 1.0e-6 mol/cm3, F = 96485 C/mol.
Using the Tafel relation eta = b log10(i/i0) with b = 0.118 V per decade, calculate the overpotential in volts needed to raise the current to ten times the exchange current density.
questions.explanation: eta = 0.118 x log10(10) = 0.118 V. One decade of current costs one Tafel slope of overpotential.

questions.question: If the anodic transfer coefficient is alpha_a = 0.60, what is the cathodic transfer coefficient alpha_c, given alpha_a + alpha_c = 1?
questions.explanation: alpha_c = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40. The two transfer coefficients sum to one.

questions.question: An electrode has an exchange current density of 1.0e-3 A/cm2 for a one-electron reaction with concentration 1.0e-5 mol/cm3. Calculate the standard rate constant k0 in cm/s, using k0 = i0/(nFC).
At large overpotentials the Butler-Volmer equation reduces to:
options: The Tafel equation, an exponential relation between current and overpotential
questions.explanation: When the overpotential is large, one of the two exponential terms dominates and Butler-Volmer becomes the Tafel equation, linear in log i versus eta.

questions.question: At equilibrium the net current is zero, but equal anodic and cathodic currents still flow.
questions.explanation: The exchange current flows in both directions at equal rates, so the net current is zero while charge transfer continues.

questions.question: Which assumptions underlie the simple Butler-Volmer treatment? Select all that apply.
options: A transfer coefficient that is constant with potential
Mass transfer that is fast enough not to limit the current
A perfect vacuum around the electrode
questions.explanation: Butler-Volmer assumes a single electron-transfer step, a roughly constant transfer coefficient, and no mass-transfer limitation. A vacuum is irrelevant to solution electrochemistry.

questions.question: A large exchange current density indicates a fast, highly reversible electrode reaction.
questions.explanation: i0 measures how readily the reaction runs in both directions; a large i0 means little overpotential is needed, characteristic of a good electrocatalyst.

questions.question: A plot of overpotential against log(current) for a reaction under kinetic control gives:
options: A straight line whose slope is the Tafel slope
questions.explanation: This Tafel plot is linear; its slope, the Tafel slope, is 2.303RT/(alpha n F) and its intercept gives the exchange current density.

questions.question: For the one-electron reaction above with k0 = 1.04e-3 cm/s and alpha = 0.5, by what factor does the forward rate constant increase when the overpotential is raised by the Tafel slope b = 0.118 V? (Answer as a factor, e.g. 10.)
questions.explanation: Raising the overpotential by one Tafel slope (2.303RT/(alpha n F)) raises log10(i/i0) by one, so the rate increases by about a factor of ten.

questions.question: The transfer coefficient alpha describes how the activation barrier changes with electrode potential.
questions.explanation: Alpha is the fraction of the applied potential change that lowers the forward activation barrier, so it sets the slope of the Tafel line.

questions.question: Using eta = b log10(i/i0) with b = 0.118 V per decade, calculate the overpotential in volts for i/i0 = 100.
questions.explanation: eta = 0.118 x log10(100) = 0.236 V. Two decades of current cost two Tafel slopes.

questions.question: For b = 0.118 V per decade, what current ratio i/i0 corresponds to an overpotential of 0.354 V?
The intercept of a Tafel plot (eta versus log i) gives:
questions.explanation: Extrapolating the Tafel line to zero overpotential gives log i0, and hence k0; the slope gives alpha.

questions.question: A larger transfer coefficient alpha produces a smaller (shallower) Tafel slope.
questions.explanation: The Tafel slope is 2.303RT/(alpha n F), so a larger alpha gives a smaller slope.

questions.question: Which conditions favour a clean Tafel line? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A clean Tafel region needs a single slow step, no mass-transfer limitation and a substantial overpotential. A slow reference would distort the measurement.
